title: Extract a Register Field
statement:
Peripheral registers rarely dedicate one bit to one meaning. A UART status
register might pack a 3-bit error code into bits 4-6, sitting between a
"data ready" flag below it and three unrelated flags above -- and reading
"that field" means shifting it down to bit 0 and masking off everything that
belongs to somebody else.

## Your function

```
unsigned int extract_field(unsigned int reg, int start, int width);
```

`start` is the position of the field's least-significant bit, `0` to `31`.
`width` is how many bits wide the field is, `1` to `32`. The field never runs
past bit 31 -- `start + width <= 32` is guaranteed by every test.

Return the field's value **right-justified**: a 1-bit field is `0` or `1`,
never `1 << start`.

`extract_field(0xF0, 4, 4)` reads bits 4-7 out of `0xF0` and returns `0xF`.

## Watch out

- **`width` can be `32`.** A field that occupies the whole register is a
  legitimate case, not one you get to skip. The obvious way to build a mask
  is `(1u << width) - 1u` -- and `1u << 32` is undefined behaviour, because
  the shift amount is not allowed to reach the bit-width of the type. It does
  not clamp or saturate in any way you can rely on: on this machine's
  compiler it comes back as `1u << 0`, so the mask you get is `0` instead of
  `0xFFFFFFFF`, and the whole register silently reads back as `0`. Give
  `width == 32` its own line.
- `reg >> start` never has this problem: `start` alone never reaches 32,
  only the mask calculation does.
